title: Pul-i Darunta: An Aramaic and Prakrit inscription
excerpt: An eight-line fragment from near Laghman combines Middle Indian phrases with Aramaic explanations and refers to several of Ashoka’s edicts.
html:
About this inscription

The Pul-i Darunta, or Lampaka, stone was found near the entrance to Afghanistan’s Laghman valley. Its eight surviving lines combine Middle Indian phrases written in Aramaic letters with Aramaic explanations. W. B. Henning identified references to several Ashokan edicts, including passages associated with rock and pillar edicts, rather than one continuous proclamation. The stone is badly broken at the start of nearly every line, so a continuous translation is impossible. Its place in the Ashokan corpus rests on those textual correspondences; it is listed as an associated inscription.

Original script

The letter groups below follow Henning’s published reading. Ellipses mark lost portions.

…𐡕𐡀 𐡐𐡈…
…𐡅𐡄 𐡋𐡀𐡍𐡔…
…𐡅𐡉 𐡎𐡄𐡉𐡕𐡉 𐡋𐡀 𐡈…
…𐡌𐡎𐡀𐡓𐡕𐡄𐡎 𐡎𐡄𐡉𐡕𐡉 𐡄𐡅…
…𐡇𐡆𐡄 𐡃𐡉𐡇𐡄𐡉𐡕𐡅𐡉 𐡎𐡄𐡉𐡕𐡉…
…𐡍𐡐𐡓𐡉𐡎 𐡀𐡁𐡄𐡉𐡎𐡉𐡕𐡎 𐡎𐡄𐡉𐡕𐡉…
…𐡓𐡉𐡔𐡅 𐡎𐡄𐡉𐡕𐡉 𐡔𐡉𐡌𐡅 𐡋𐡌𐡊𐡕𐡁 𐡁𐡏𐡌…
…𐡀𐡇𐡓𐡉𐡍 𐡄𐡅𐡃𐡏𐡍…

Roman transliteration

1. …tʾ pṭ…
2. …wh lʾnš…
3. …wy shyty lʾ ṭ…
4. …msʾrths shyty hw…
5. …ḥzh dḥhytwy shyty…
6. …nprys ʾbhysyts shyty…
7. …ryšw shyty šymw lmktb bʿm…
8. …ʾḥryn hwdʿn…

English translation

The breaks are too large to recover complete sentences. The following gives the sense of the surviving words and the source parallels Henning identified; suggested edict numbers are scholarly identifications, not numbers engraved on this stone.

1–2. … [damaged words concerning living beings and people] … 3. … “in accordance with” … [part of a cited Indian phrase] … 4. … “in accordance with” … [a phrase Henning compared with a rock edict] … 5. … “to see” … “in accordance with” … [another edict phrase] … 6. … “the Beloved of the Gods, consecrated” … “in accordance with” … 7. … “in accordance with” … “they ordered [it] to be written” … 8. … “others” … “made known” …

Henning connected the surviving phrases with several longer edicts, among them Major Rock Edict XIII. The fragment does not preserve those complete edicts; the pages for the numbered edicts give their separate surviving versions.

Sources

  • W. B. Henning, “The Aramaic Inscription of Asoka found in Lampāka” (1949), Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 13(1), pp. 80–88 (transcription and analysis).
  • Harry Falk, Aśokan Sites and Artefacts (2006), pp. 251–252 (site history and translation of the surviving portions).
